prize_parts.citation: for showing how borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices to amplify and propagate economic fluctuations

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B050. I now prefer B002, confined to Kiyotaki and Moore. The change comes from re-applying my own criteria to the exchange, not from the count of members who ranked B002 first. Those criteria are a clear and original mechanism, a credible link to evidence, maturity, and exact credit. The 1997 Kiyotaki-Moore paper is a two-author origin of one mechanism: collateral values and borrowing limits feed back on each other, so temporary shocks become persistent and amplified. It has nearly three decades of theoretical, quantitative and policy use, and no member has disputed its maturity or its originality. On exact credit it is the cleanest candidate on the shortlist. B050 is weaker on that criterion. Besley's inclusion is the most debatable attribution there, and my own round-1 reservation was that the cross-country identification of electoral and constitutional effects is thinner than the theory's influence. I hold B002 to the same identification standard, and the gap between theory and direct evidence on the size of amplification is real there as well. But B002's claim is the existence and logic of a propagation mechanism, with credit that does not depend on a contested split. B050's claim leans more heavily on empirical results whose causal reading I question. B025 has the stronger firm-level evidence base, but the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum omission is a larger attribution problem than anything in B002. I keep Gertler out. His accelerator work has Bernanke as a co-originator and is divided with B043. The two-name citation is narrower and more defensible.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the empirical identification of collateral-driven amplification is weaker than the theory's influence. Several colleagues note that the quantitative size of the effect is debated. As someone who weights credibility-revolution standards, I should not wave this away. A prize here would reward a mechanism whose empirical magnitude is not well pinned down. A second reservation is adjacency to the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises. I regard it as thematic, not as duplication of the discovery, but I cannot verify the exact scope of that prize beyond what colleagues state. A third is that the two-name version leaves the financial-accelerator strand (Gertler, Gilchrist) unrecognised, and a reader could see the citation as narrower than the literature. Finally, I am moving away from a candidate I ranked first at opening, and that should be read as a reassessment of attribution and identification, not as a vote-counting move. B050 remains scientifically coherent, and its 2024 adjacency is a balance issue, not a merit demerit.

responses.point: Hassler prefers Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler, centring the award on collateral constraints while crediting the broader finding that financial frictions propagate fluctuations. He accepts two names as a fallback if the accelerator lineage is judged too close to the 2022 recognition.
responses.response: I accept that Gertler's later intermediary-based work with Kiyotaki and with Karadi is separable from the 2022 recognition, and that the three-name version is a coherent broader citation. I still prefer two names. His credit is divided between B002 and the eight-name B043, and the accelerator lineage has a co-originator who is already a laureate. The supplied materials give me no way to say how credit on the intermediary strand divides between him and his co-authors, so I would not write that into a citation. Your fallback is the version I support. I also note that you are the chair and the only member whose preferred part includes Gertler, so I weigh your three-name case on its arguments.

responses.point: Boppart argues that the overlap with the 2022 prize is thematic and not a duplication. The prize concerned banks, runs and intermediation, whereas Kiyotaki-Moore concerns collateral values on borrowers' balance sheets creating a dynamic feedback loop. He also says the accelerator rests on agency costs and external finance premia, so it is a different achievement.
responses.response: This is the argument that moves me most on overlap, and it is the reverse of how I treated B050's adjacency to the 2024 prize in round 1. I applied the same principle there: adjacency is something for the Committee to weigh, not duplication, when the mechanism and outcome differ. I now apply it to B002 too. I agree that the collateral-asset price loop is a distinct mechanism. I cannot confirm from the supplied evidence how far the 2022 laureates' work touched it, so I leave the residual risk in my uncertainties. I share your reservation that direct identification of the amplification magnitude is the weak point.

responses.point: Teorell proposes a two-part configuration: Kiyotaki and Moore for B002, and Pakes alone for B012, which stays under the three-person cap by dropping Gertler, Berry and Levinsohn. He records that omitting Berry and Levinsohn is a real attribution loss.
responses.response: I agree with your two-name B002 and with your own stated cost for the B012 part. I would not add Pakes alone. BLP is a joint contribution, and a single-name part that omits Berry and Levinsohn would misdescribe where the demand-estimation breakthrough came from. Pairing macro-finance with empirical IO also has no common theme, as you acknowledge. I am not objecting to B012's merit. Reach and maturity are not in doubt, and I would regard a clean three-name B012 as a serious option. My objection is to the specific pairing that the cap forces. I would rather present a single, well-bounded part.

responses.point: Enflo disagrees with my round-1 B021 proposal of Autor and Hanson only. She argues that Dorn co-authored the central China-shock papers and the later work on local adjustment, so a two-name award would misdescribe where the discovery came from. She agrees that Katz should not be credited.
responses.response: I accept this correction. If B021 were chosen, dropping Dorn would be arbitrary for a citation confined to the trade-shock core. Her narrowing of the citation also answers my concern about Acemoglu and Restrepo and the Goldin-Katz overlap on the task strand. I ranked B021 fifth at opening and am not moving it up. I am more persuaded than before that a decade of re-examination is meaningful maturity for empirical work, and she is right that the debate concerns magnitudes. I still see persistence and shift-share identification as unresolved enough to keep it behind B002 on exact credit, but I no longer count Dorn's inclusion against it.

uncertainties: How strongly direct evidence supports quantitatively large collateral amplification. I hold B002 to the same identification standard I applied to B050, and I have not independently verified the empirical literature.
How much of the collateral-constraint mechanism the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises covers. I rely on colleagues' descriptions of that prize.
Whether the two-name citation looks incomplete relative to the financial-accelerator literature, given Gertler and Gilchrist, and how credit in that lineage divides.

Whether B050's Besley inclusion and cross-country identification concerns would be settled better by the Committee than by my reading, and whether the 2024 adjacency is a merit or only a balance matter.

Whether the Committee should weigh a mechanism with clean credit above a candidate with firmer firm-level evidence but an attribution gap (B025). I judge exact credit to decide here, but this is a judgment call.
I have not independently verified citation counts, publication dates or the scope of prior prizes. I rely on the shortlist text and colleagues' stated recollections.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the preferred part B002 or the alternatives B050 and B025. Kiyotaki, Moore, Persson, Tabellini, Besley, Helpman and Melitz are not among my listed co-authors. My profile records an institutional overlap at Stockholm University (2010-17) with the IIES macro group, including Hassler and Krusell, who prefer B002. It is not a co-authorship, and I disclose it without adjudicating it. In round 1 I treated Teorell's reported past co-authorship with Torsten Persson as real. His own conflict note says the supplied profile does not support that identification, so I now treat it as unverified. It bears only on B050, which is no longer my preferred part. My work is in labour, education and immigration economics, which is adjacent to none of the B002 names.
